title: PAROXYSMAL EXTREME PAIN DISORDER
alt_titles: PAIN, SUBMANDIBULAR, OCULAR, AND RECTAL, WITH FLUSHING

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that paroxysmal extreme pain disorder (PEXPD) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SCN9A gene (603415) on chromosome 2q24.3.

checks.claim: Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder (PEXPD) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SCN9A gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder (PEPD) is a rare autosomal dominant pain disorder linked to a mutation in the SCN9A gene, which encodes voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.7.
checks.explanation: The abstract calls PEPD an autosomal dominant disorder caused by SCN9A mutation. It also reports a heterozygous pathogenic SCN9A mutation in the patient.

checks.evidence_quote: mutational analysis of the candidate gene SCN9A, which encodes hNa(v)1.7
checks.explanation: The abstract does not give the chromosomal location. Under the instructions, a gene's standard location counts as nomenclature restating the paper.

paragraphs.text: Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder is an inherited condition characterized by paroxysms of rectal, ocular, or submandibular pain with flushing (Fertleman et al., 2006). Hayden and Grossman (1959) described it as a familial autonomic disorder. According to Fertleman et al. (2007), onset is in the neonatal period or infancy and the disorder persists throughout life. It is characterized by attacks of excruciating deep burning pain, often in the rectal, ocular, or jaw areas, triggered by factors such as defecation, cold wind, eating, and emotion. Harlequin color change and tonic attacks occur, and dramatic syncopes with bradycardia and sometimes asystole are common (Fertleman et al., 2007). The disorder was formerly called familial rectal pain syndrome (Fertleman and Ferrie, 2006).

paragraphs.text: Fertleman et al. (2007) gave a detailed clinical description of 77 individuals from 15 families with paroxysmal extreme pain disorder. Autonomic manifestations predominated at first, including skin flushing, harlequin color change, and tonic attacks. Dramatic syncopes with bradycardia and sometimes asystole were common. Later, the disorder was characterized by attacks of excruciating deep burning pain, often in the rectal, ocular, or jaw areas. Attacks were triggered by factors such as defecation, cold wind, eating, and emotion. Carbamazepine was effective in almost all patients who tried it, although the response was often incomplete.

paragraphs.text: Fertleman et al. (2006) carried out mutational analysis of the candidate gene SCN9A, which encodes the sodium channel Nav1.7. In 11 families and 2 sporadic cases with paroxysmal extreme pain disorder, they identified 8 missense mutations. Functional analysis in vitro of mutant Nav1.7 channels showed a reduction in fast inactivation, leading to a persistent sodium current. Fertleman et al. (2006) contrasted this with other SCN9A mutations, which cause primary erythermalgia and are associated with more negative activation thresholds.
